approved: Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers Fees Imposition Bill 2015
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill is part of a package that also includes the Register of Foreign Ownership of Agricultural Land Bill 2015 and the Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers Legislation Amendment Bill 2015.
The package would create a Register of foreign ownership of agricultural land, to be run by the Commissioner, with a public statistical part and a full basic part kept confidential.

The Commissioner must give the Minister an annual report on the Register's operation, and the Act would be treated as a taxation law so existing confidentiality rules in the Taxation Administration Act 1953 apply.
Establishes a Register of foreign ownership of agricultural land.
Requires the Commissioner to publish a statistical part of the Register online.
Requires the Commissioner to report annually to the Minister on the Register's operation.
Foreign persons who hold interests in agricultural land in Australia, the Commissioner, and the Minister.

The Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers Fees Imposition Bill 2015 introduces fees on foreign investment applications, shifting administration and enforcement costs from taxpayers to investors. For residential and agricultural properties valued at $1 million or less, the fee is $5,000, with higher fees for more expensive properties and commercial or business applications.

The speaker argued that the government strongly supports foreign investment but needs to know where it is and ensure it serves Australia's national interest. They highlighted that the Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers Legislation Amendment Bill 2015 overhauls four-decade-old rules, increases criminal penalties from $90,000 to $135,000 for individuals, gives the ATO responsibility for regulating residential real estate investment, and lowers screening thresholds for agricultural investments.

The speaker supported the three foreign investment bills, which introduce fees on applications to shift administrative costs from taxpayers, increase penalties for noncompliance, lower the agricultural land screening threshold to $15 million, and strengthen ATO enforcement, but expressed concern about applying different screening thresholds for investors from different countries.

The speaker argued that the bills strengthen regulation of foreign investment in agricultural land, agribusiness and residential real estate, introducing a register for acquisitions over $15 million, FIRB review for agribusiness purchases over $55 million, higher penalties and application fees expected to net $620 million, and raising the substantial interest threshold from 15% to 20%.

The speech argued that the government's foreign investment bills are insufficient to fix housing affordability, criticised the demonisation of foreign and Asian-Australian buyers, and noted that foreign investment is essential for the economy and agricultural sector. The speaker cited Reserve Bank data showing foreign residential purchases are about two per cent of transactions and accused the government of xenophobic rhetoric.

The member for Robertson supported the Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers amendment bills, which tighten foreign investment rules with stricter penalties, lower agricultural screening thresholds, a register of foreign ownership, and $47.5 million for ATO enforcement—reporting over 500 foreign-owned residential properties under investigation and supporting the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement for local jobs.

The minister argued that the Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers bills modernise the foreign investment regime and fulfil an election commitment, while praising the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement as the best deal either country has made, opening a market of 1.35 billion people.

The speaker supported three bills to strengthen Australia's foreign investment framework, including lowering the agricultural land screening threshold to $15 million (with higher thresholds for US, New Zealand and Chilean investors), establishing a register of foreign-owned agricultural land, and increasing penalties for non-compliance. The bills also introduce application fees and transfer residential real estate regulation to the Australian Taxation Office, with $47.5 million allocated for compliance.

The member argued in favour of the Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers bills, citing examples of beneficial foreign investment in his electorate including New Forests' purchase of a mill at Tarpeena and Hassad Australia's acquisition of Telopea Downs, and welcomed new thresholds lowering the Foreign Investment Review Board referral for agricultural land from $252 million to a cumulative $15 million, with a $55 million threshold for agribusinesses.

The member supported the foreign investment package, citing reduced screening thresholds of $15 million for agricultural land and $55 million for agribusiness, plus a new foreign ownership register from 1 July 2015. They also defended the China-Australia free trade agreement, noting Chinese property investment on the Gold Coast totalled $148 million in 2013–14, and criticised federal Labor's opposition to it.
Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers Fees Imposition Act 2015
